deleteList.why: The package was one flattened module, so an eager import of any part of it made the whole library reachable from the initial bundle. A dynamic import of the package was the only lever that moved it out, and it paid for that with an async boundary in the consumer's own code. Each component is now its own entry point, so a plain static import lands in the chunk that uses it. Still legitimate where the lazy boundary exists for its own sake — a feature area deliberately kept off the critical path.
deleteList.replaceWith: a static import from the component's own entry point, e.g. @ids-group-ltd/ids-design-system/toast

informational: Every component is now its own entry point: @ids-group-ltd/ids-design-system/button, /table, /toast and 66 more resolve alongside the package root, which still exports everything it did. No import has to change.

The root facade costs nothing: the same app measured 138.36 kB gzip importing each component from its own entry point and 138.37 kB importing them all from the root. Both spellings resolve to the same file, so one component imported two ways is one class and instanceof holds across them.

A longer form of each specifier also resolves, naming the folder the component lives in (@ids-group-ltd/ids-design-system/components/button). The short one is the supported spelling; the long one exists because it is the name the package build derives.

37 internal helpers, base classes and shared types became importable because an entry point must export whatever another entry point imports — devWarn, DsFieldBase, ds-calendar-day and the like. Each carries @internal, none appears in the component reference, and none is covered by the versioning promise: they can change or disappear in any release. Build on what the reference documents.
